candidate.answerReason: The stopping chip is white exactly when the fifth chip in an imagined complete draw order is red. Each chip is equally likely to be fifth, giving probability 3/5 and choice D.

methods.label: Imagine the complete draw order
methods.explanation:
Imagine continuing the random draws until all five chips have been removed. This preserves every draw made before the original stopping rule takes effect, and it lets us relate that rule to the fifth chip.

If the fifth chip is red, both white chips occur before it. When the second white is drawn, at least that final red chip remains, so the original process stops on white.

If the fifth chip is white, all three red chips occur before it. When the third red is drawn, at least that final white chip remains, so the original process stops on red.

Thus the last chip actually drawn is white exactly when the fifth chip in the complete order is red. Each of the five physical chips is equally likely to occupy the fifth position, and three are red. The required probability is therefore \(\boxed{\frac35}\), choice \(\mathrm{D}\).
methods.levelReason: Uses equally likely positions in a random draw order and an exhaustive two-case explanation of the stopping rule.

candidate.annotationRationale: The target is an exact probability in a finite equally likely model. The method identifies an equivalent event determined by the final position and counts three favorable chips out of five. Sampling without replacement and recognizing equal likelihood support the argument; independence and conditional-probability calculations are not used.

review.mathematicalCheck: In a completed draw order, a final red chip prevents red exhaustion until after both whites occur, so the original process stops on white. A final white similarly forces stopping on red. Each physical chip is equally likely to be fifth, giving probability 3/5.
review.levelCheck: The finite probability argument is elementary. Both cases explain the stopping-event equivalence completely.
